question: How many days per year am I allowed to work as an international student in Germany without asking the employment agency?
answer:
If you are from a non-EU country, you can generally work 140 full days or 280 half days per calendar year without approval from the Employment Agency [S1][S2][S5][S7]. Part-time student jobs at your university are also allowed on top of this [S1][S3], and research assistants at universities are exempt from the limit but must still inform the immigration office [S7]. To work more, you need approval from the employment agency and the foreigners' office [S7]. Working beyond 140 days without a permit may lead to a fine of up to 5000 euros [S4]. Students from the EU, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland have unrestricted access to the labour market [S2].

Note that the sources disagree: a BAMF brochure gives a lower limit of 120 full or 240 half days [S8]. Most sources, including Hamburg's 2024 guide, state 140 days [S1]. The retrieval dates don't show which is newer, so please confirm the current limit with your local foreigners' office. This is not legal advice.

question: Can international students in Türkiye work part-time, and does it depend on whether they are bachelor's or master's students?
answer: Yes, but not on your student residence permit alone: you first need a separate work permit [S1][S3]. According to METU, you cannot apply for it yourself; you first find a job, and the employer applies for your permit [S3]. The rules do depend on your level of study. If you are an associate or bachelor's student, you can work part-time only after completing your first year [S2][S3]. If you are a master's or PhD student, that first-year limit does not apply [S2]; you can get a permit from your first year, for full-time or part-time jobs [S3]. Graduate students may also work as researchers in projects related to their studies [S1]. METU states that permits at both levels are only for jobs outside the university or campus [S3]. Applications for unrelated jobs in entertainment or domestic work are evaluated negatively [S2]. If you are a Türkiye Scholarships holder, the YTB is consulted [S2]. Rules can change, so confirm with the Ministry of Labour or your university's international office.

question: How long does the migration office in Izmir currently take to process a first student residence permit?
answer: The sources don't give current processing times for the Izmir migration office specifically. They only describe national rules and practice at Istanbul and Ankara universities. Sabancı University (Istanbul) says that, under Directorate General of Migration Management rules, processing takes 30–90 days after your application is received for evaluation [S6]. Results are announced via email/SMS and the e-ikamet website [S2]. You can check your status on e-ikamet by choosing "first application" [S1][S3], or call 157 [S1]. Your card is sent to the address on your application [S1]. Whether Izmir is currently faster or slower isn't covered. Please confirm with your university's international office or the Izmir Provincial Directorate of Migration Management; this is not legal advice.

question: After I find a place to live in Germany, what local step should I do before applying for my residence permit?
answer: You should first register your address at the local Residents' Registration Office (Einwohnermeldeamt, in some cities called Bürgerbüro or Bezirksamt) [S1][S3]. Key points: Timing: register within one week according to one passage [S1], or within one or two weeks depending on local requirements according to another; otherwise you could be fined. If no appointment is available in time, what matters is that you booked one within that period, usually online [S3]. Process: you fill out a registration form and receive a written confirmation of registration (Meldebestätigung) [S1]. Keep it, because you need it to apply for your residence permit at the foreigners' registration office [S1][S3]. Next step: apply for the permit as soon as you have registered your address, and at least 6 weeks before your visa expires [S2]. Rules vary by city, so please confirm with your local office; this is not legal advice.

question: Can I start attending classes at a German university before completing its enrolment process?
answer: No. You are only allowed to attend courses at a German university once you are officially enrolled (matriculated) [S1][S5]. Accepting a study place is not enough: you officially become a student only when you enrol [S2]. After enrolment you can start attending classes and take exams [S3]. Practical steps: Your letter of acceptance gives the enrolment procedure, dates and required documents (typically proof of health insurance, semester fee receipt, passport photo, ID/passport) [S3]. Enrolment deadlines are often short, and if you are late or forget documents you will not be able to enrol [S6]. In many cases you must enrol in person, so arrive in Germany before the deadline [S2]. Please confirm details with your university's international or admissions office; this is not legal advice.

question: When do I have to show proof of health insurance as an international student in Germany?
answer: You must show proof of health insurance when you enrol (register) at your German university, and also when you apply for a residence permit [S4]. Depending on your country of origin, you may already need to prove coverage when you apply for a visa [S1]. For example, a German consulate checklist for the Netherlands asks visa applicants to bring confirmation of German health insurance [S7]. Universities such as RWTH Aachen make proof of valid health insurance mandatory for enrolment, and you must contact a statutory health insurer before you enrol [S2]. At LMU Munich, a German public health insurer sends your insurance status to the university electronically [S5]. If your home insurance is recognised, get an exemption confirmation from a German health insurer after arriving but before enrolling [S6]. It's best to sort this out as early as possible [S1]. Rules can change, so confirm the details with your university and the responsible authority; this is not legal advice.

question: What does the German residence permit card store on its chip?
answer: Your German residence permit card (the electronic residence title, 'elektronischer Aufenthaltstitel' or eAT) has an integrated chip that stores certain data about you, for example your passport photo and your fingerprints [S4][S2]. The DAAD guide simply says the chip stores "certain information about you" without listing it in full [S1]. question: If I am an international student in Türkiye, can I wait until my visa expires before starting the residence permit application?
answer: No, you should not wait until after your visa expires. You must complete your e-ikamet application before your residence permit, visa, or visa-free stay period expires, and the Migration Office goes by your online application date [S2]. For a first application, ITU says to apply within the legal period of stay after you enter the country. For example, that means within 1 month on a 1-month visa, or within 3 months if you have a 3-month visa exemption [S5]. Practical tips: enter your full residential address accurately, and do not use your university's address as your residence address, or your application may be rejected [S5]. If documents are missing, the Migration Directorate may give you up to 30 days to complete them. If you don't deliver them on time, your application will be removed from processing [S6]. This is not legal advice, so please confirm deadlines with your university's international office or the Migration Office.

question: What is the Turkish foreign national identity number used for at METU besides identifying me?
answer: At METU, your foreign national identity number is used in the Student Affairs Information System (SAIS). SAIS requires it when you request your end-of-semester grades, when you request a student certificate, and when you graduate [S1]. Without it, you won't be able to see your grades, get student certificates or graduate [S1]. If you haven't submitted it yet, give it to the responsible International Students' advisor at the Registrar's Office [S1]. You can find the number on your residence permit card, or look it up at https://tckimlik.nvi.gov.tr/ [S1]. The number also matters for health insurance. If you want General Health Insurance (GSS), you must apply immediately after getting the number [S1]. The GSS application needs a student certificate showing your foreigner identification number [S3]. This isn't legal advice, so please confirm the details with METU's Registrar's Office.

question: If I graduate from a Turkish higher education program and want to remain to look for work, what permit might I apply for?
answer: You can apply for a short-term residence permit under the "those who graduated from a Turkish university" category, which gives about one year to look for work in Türkiye [S1][S7]. Key conditions: - Apply within six months after graduation [S1][S7]; METU adds that this must be before your student residence permit expires [S4]. - If your student card's expiry date is after your graduation date, you may stay until that date [S4]; otherwise you must leave within 10 days after your student card expires [S7]. - The permit can be extended for one more year if you apply before it expires or within 90 days after expiry [S1]. - Each new graduation (undergraduate, master's, PhD) gives a separate right to apply [S4]. Note that to actually work, you need a separate work permit [S6]. These sources are university guidance, not legal advice; confirm details with the Migration Office (e.g. by calling 157) [S7].

question: How much money do I need in my blocked account for a German student visa?
answer: For a regular student visa, most sources say you need €992 per month, i.e. €11,904 for your first year [S1][S4][S6]. The DAAD notes the old amount of €11,208 rose to €11,904 from January 2025 [S7], so the Netherlands sheet's €934/month (€11,208) appears outdated [S3]. Munich also cites at least €11,904 [S8]. The sources disagree on higher figures. The Taipei checklist asks for €13,092 (12 x €1,091), with withdrawals capped at €1,027 per month [S5]. The Tanzania page applies €1,091 per month (€13,092 per year) to applicants without an admission letter, such as those seeking studies [S4]. Open the account before you apply, and bring the official opening confirmation showing the total paid in and the monthly amount [S4]. A scholarship covering €992 per month, or a Verpflichtungserklärung, can replace the account [S1]. All sources were retrieved on the same date. This isn't legal advice, so please confirm the exact amount with the German mission handling your application.

question: If I want to freelance while studying in Germany as an international student, is the usual student work allowance enough by itself?
answer: No, not if you are from a non-EU country. The standard allowance of 140 full days or 280 half days a year covers ordinary jobs, but self-employed or freelance work is only possible if the Ausländerbehörde (foreigners' office) permits it [S3]. The DAAD guide says such work is evaluated case by case [S4]. In Hamburg, you apply for this permit at the Foreigners Registration Department. It may be granted only if it does not jeopardise completing your studies [S1]. Freelancing beyond the 140-day rule is usually allowed only for work in a limited timescale [S1]. Freelancing without a permit can bring a fine of up to 5,000 euros and put your residence right at risk [S1]. Students from the EU may work self-employed without restriction [S8]. The Hamburg details come from one city's guide, so other cities may differ. This is not legal advice; please confirm with your local foreigners' office.

question: Can students from outside the EU simply exceed the German student work-day limit if they find more shifts?
answer: No. As a non-EU student you may work 140 full days or 280 half days per calendar year without approval [S3][S6]. If you want to work more, you need approval from the employment agency and the immigration office (Ausländerbehörde) [S3][S4]. Sources describe this permission as limited: DAAD says it is granted only in cases of special financial need [S4], and TUM says exceptions are made only in individual cases, with no automatic right [S1]. Working beyond 140 days off campus without a permit can bring a fine of up to 5,000 euros and a check on revoking your residence permit [S8]. Both you and your employer must check whether the 140 days are used up [S8]. The limit resets only in January, not when you extend your permit [S2]. Part-time on-campus student jobs are allowed throughout the year [S1][S6], and research assistants at universities are exempt but must inform the immigration office [S3]. This is not legal advice; confirm with your Foreigners' Office.

question: I am coming to Türkiye on an exchange lasting one semester. Do I need a residence permit?
answer:
Most likely yes. You need a residence permit if you will stay in Türkiye longer than 90 days, and one source says this applies to all Erasmus students when they arrive [S7]. If your semester, including any time before or after classes, lasts more than 90 days, plan to apply. The sources do not say how long a semester is, so check your exact dates.

Key points:
- For Erasmus students, the permit covers the length of the exchange and is issued without a fee [S6].
- If you need to stay longer, apply for an extension through the e-Residence system before your permit ends [S6].
- Applications are decided within 90 days at the latest, and while your application is pending you may stay legally [S6].
- Use only the documents officially listed by your host university, and book an appointment with its office [S7].

This is not legal advice. Please confirm with your host university and the Migration Office.

question: If my Turkish visa allows a longer visit, can I stay more than 90 days in any 180-day period?
answer:
No. With a visa you can stay in Türkiye a maximum of 90 days within 180 days, even if the visa itself is valid for longer, such as one year [S4]. question: How many hours per week may I work in Germany before I have to pay the same insurance contributions as German students?
answer: The threshold is 20 hours per week. All students in Germany may work up to 20 hours a week during the lecture period and still count as students for social security [S3]. Above that, you count as an employee and must pay earnings-related health, pension and unemployment insurance contributions [S3][S2]. Even below 20 hours, students usually pay low contributions, but only if they earn more than 556 EUR per month [S4]. Short jobs are exempt: you pay no social security contributions if you work less than three months at a stretch or less than 70 days a year [S4][S7]. If you are from outside the EU/EEA, you are also limited to 140 full days or 280 half days a year without approval [S8]. Working that much can also put your student residence permit at risk if it harms your studies [S3]. This is not legal advice, so confirm details with your health insurer or the immigration office.

question: My German D visa runs out soon. When do I need to apply for the residence permit?
answer:
Apply as soon as possible, and well before your D visa expires. The exact deadline depends on your local Foreigners' Office, and the sources differ:

In Berlin, the official Service Berlin page says you apply only online, and no earlier than 4 months before your current title expires [S6]. All sources were retrieved on the same date, so check your own city's office.

Once you have applied, you can stay in Germany while you wait for your appointment, even if your visa expires ("Fiktionswirkung") [S2][S3]. Keep your visa and the office's confirmation as proof [S2].

This is not legal advice; confirm the deadline with your local Foreigners' Office.

question: If I have private health insurance in Germany, can I later switch to statutory insurance during my studies?
answer:
It depends on how your private insurance is set up. If you use private insurance to be exempted from statutory insurance, you generally cannot switch to statutory insurance during your studies [S1][S6]. Once a statutory provider issues the exemption confirmation, you are no longer allowed to join German public health insurance for the rest of your studies [S6].

Private cover that only bridges the time before enrolment is different. Statutory student insurance can only start after you take up residence and enrol, so you need private insurance until then [S5]. An Incoming-Health Insurance Package lets you move without a gap into long-term student insurance with a statutory or private provider [S7].

The sources mainly describe home-country private insurance and the exemption process. Please confirm your own case with your insurer or a statutory provider before you decide. This is not legal advice.

question: How much should I budget per month for accommodation as a student in Türkiye?
answer:
According to Study in Türkiye, you should reserve between 215 TL and 2500 TL per month for accommodation, depending on whether you choose a state, university or private dormitory or a rental flat [S1]. Private dormitories usually offer better facilities than state dormitories but cost more [S7]. Rental prices vary by city, location and the characteristics of the house [S7].

Key points:
- You pay dormitories monthly and do not pay in summer when you are not staying there. Rent for a flat, however, is paid all 12 months [S1].
- Both dormitories and rental apartments require a deposit when you first move in, linked to the monthly fee or rent [S1].
- If you hold a Türkiye Scholarship, accommodation is provided [S6]. Eligible graduate students can receive cash accommodation aid of 750 TL per month [S2].

The sources do not say how current these figures are, so check them with your university's accommodation office or the responsible authority before you plan.

question: How many years can a German graduate's post-study residence permit be extended beyond its initial 18-month job-search period?
answer: It can't be extended at all for job search. The post-study job-search permit runs for up to 18 months, and you cannot extend it beyond 18 months to keep looking for work [S2][S3]. After that, a new residence permit can only be issued for a different purpose of stay [S2]. For example, if you find an appropriate job within the 18 months, you can get a residence permit for employment [S5]. If you later earn a new degree, you may again apply for an 18-month job-search permit [S7]. Rules can change, so please confirm your situation with your local Foreigners Registration Office. This is not legal advice.

question: Can I get a German residence permit just to do an intensive English course?
answer: No. According to the sources, a German residence permit cannot be issued for an intensive course to learn a foreign language such as English [S1][S3]. Intensive German courses taken for this purpose must run at least 18 hours a week and must not be publicly funded [S1]. If you want to come mainly to learn German, a separate short-term intensive language course option exists, requiring daily instruction of at least 18 hours per week and secured means of subsistence [S5]. Please confirm your situation with the German mission or the responsible foreigners' authority, as this is not legal advice and rules can change.

question: Who applies for my work permit in Türkiye, me or my employer?
answer:
Your employer applies, not you. As a student, a work permit is not something you can apply for individually; the company that wants to hire you applies for your work permit, so you first need to find a job [S6]. The MFA describes a process where you apply at the nearest Turkish mission with your passport, visa application form and a letter from your employer, and your employer then submits the other documents to the Ministry of Labour and Social Security within ten working days [S2][S3]. The Ministry finalizes applications within thirty days at the latest [S2].

Key conditions for students: undergraduates can get a permit only after their first year and only for part-time jobs off campus; graduate students can from their first year, full- or part-time, off campus [S6]. Your residence permit alone does not give you the right to work [S6].

This is not legal advice; please confirm with the Ministry of Labour or your university's international office.
